sentences.text: Antarctopelta was a medium-sized, stocky quadruped that reached at least four meters in length. It was a herbivore protected by skin-embedded armor plates, a defensive feature shared with other ankylosaurians.
The tail likely ended in a macuahuitl, a cluster of spiked osteoderms resembling an Aztec weapon, similar to the structure found in its relative Stegouros.

The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is the only known material of the genus. This single fossil consists of approximately fifteen percent of the skeleton, including skull fragments, vertebrae, limb bones, and armor pieces.
A 2019 histological analysis revealed that the individual represented by the holotype was sexually mature.
Bone growth rates in Antarctopelta remained consistent despite different climatic conditions compared to lower latitude ankylosaurs.
The discovery of a shark tooth and bivalves with the specimen suggests the animal died and floated out to sea, a behavior seen in other ankylosaurs.
The only known specimen was discovered in 1986 by Argentine geologists Eduardo Olivero and Robert Scasso on James Ross Island in the Antarctic Peninsula.
It was the second dinosaur formally named from Antarctica, following Cryolophosaurus in 1994, and the genus was named by Salgado and Gasparini in 2006.
Five cervical vertebrae were initially discovered, but three were lost after being molded with latex.
Despite being preserved in a marine environment, Antarctopelta is similar to other ankylosaurians that lived on land.
It possibly coexisted with the ornithopod Trinisaura.
The ecosystem also included mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and sharks.
Antarctopelta is the only known ankylosaur from Antarctica and belongs to the subfamily Parankylosauria.
A 2011 phylogenetic analysis suggested that Antarctopelta is the most basal known nodosaurid, a finding supported by a new analysis by Thompson et al. in 2011.
However, it shares traits with both ankylosaurids and nodosaurids, making family assignment difficult so it has been designated as Ankylosauria incertae sedis.
Antarctopelta lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Campanian stage, from approximately 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The holotype skeleton was found about 90 meters from the base of the Gamma Member of the Snow Hill Island Formation.
During Antarctopelta's time, Earth was warmer and humider, leaving Antarctica ice-free.
It is debated whether the individual was immature based on bone fusion, as histological analysis suggests it was sexually mature.
